# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
# Review of "Reduced Working Time at Full Pay" (Working Paper 24-07)

The arithmetic is internally consistent:
- The sector rows sum to 61 organisations and 2,940 employees.
- The employee-weighted output index works out to 98.73.
- Each "per-hour" figure is the index divided by 0.8.
- The secondary-outcome percentages are correct.

The problems are in what the numbers are taken to show. The headline conclusion that the model is sector-general is contradicted by the paper's own data.

---

## 1. The per-hour "gains" are guaranteed by the arithmetic

Output per scheduled hour is defined as the output index divided by 0.8. Any index above 80 therefore shows a per-hour "gain". An organisation whose output fell by 15% would still report +6%.

So the claims that there were "gains in every sector" and that the result showed "size and consistency" (which the Limitations section relies on) tell us almost nothing. They follow from the fact that no sector lost more than 20% of output. The informative number is the **output index itself**, and it tells a more modest story:

- Five of six sectors finished **below** baseline, so the "100% of the output" deal was not met overall.
- **Retail and hospitality lost 6.9% of output.** That is the real result for the sector where output is most tied to hours. Reporting it as "+16.4% per hour" turns a loss into an apparent success.

## 2. The continuation data contradict "sector-general"

All five reverting organisations came from the two weakest sectors:

| Sector | Orgs | Reverted | Reversion rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Retail & hospitality | 6 | 3 | **50%** |
| Healthcare admin | 5 | 2 | **40%** |
| Other four sectors | 50 | 0 | 0% |

Half of the retail and hospitality organisations abandoned the model, and these are the customer-facing sector the Discussion singles out as proof of generality. Combined with output losses of 3.5–7%, the evidence points the **opposite** way: the model held up in knowledge work and struggled in coverage-dependent work.

The aggregate "92% continued" figure hides this pattern, even though the Results section reports the breakdown. Note also that n = 6 and n = 5 are too small to support a claim of generality either way.

## 3. Sick days: part of the fall is mechanical and part may be seasonal

- **Fewer working days.** On a four-day week there are 20% fewer scheduled days on which to take sick leave. If sickness were unchanged per working day, sick days per year would fall from 4.4 to about 3.5 automatically. Roughly 20 of the 36 percentage points of reduction need no behavioural explanation. Sick days per scheduled day is the right measure.
- **Seasonality.** Revenue was compared with the same months of the previous year "to remove seasonality", but output and sick days were compared with the **preceding six months**. Recruitment was in early 2023 and was followed by two months of preparation, so the baseline period probably covered autumn and winter, which is flu season, while the pilot ran through spring and summer. That alone could lower sick days, and it may also affect output. The paper should state the actual dates and apply the same seasonal adjustment it used for revenue.
- **Annualisation.** Both rates are annualised from six months, which magnifies any short-term fluctuation.

## 4. Resignations

People are unlikely to quit a job during the first six months of a new and valued perk, especially before they know whether it will be made permanent. That is an anticipation effect, not evidence of lasting retention. The 2023 labour market also cooled considerably compared with 2022. Without a comparison group, neither explanation can be ruled out.

## 5. Revenue is probably a real-terms decline

Revenue is reported in nominal terms. Inflation in 2022–23 was well above 1.4% in most advanced economies, so nominal growth of 1.4% very likely means **real revenue fell**. In addition:
- 9 of the 61 organisations, about 15%, did not report revenue, and we are not told which ones.
- Non-profit "revenue" (donations and grants) is not output.

The statement that revenue "offers no sign that output was sacrificed" is not supported.

## 6. The primary outcome is weak, and its weakness affects every sector at once

The output index was:
- reported by managers who ran the pilot and had publicly signed up to the "100% output" goal;
- built from "whatever records" each organisation held, so it is not comparable across organisations;
- not audited, and reported with no dispersion, no confidence intervals and no organisation-level distribution.

Values clustered just below 100 are exactly what you would expect if invested managers were anchoring on the target. Consistency across sectors does not reduce this concern. A bias shared by every manager produces consistency, so the Limitations section's reasoning ("unlikely to overturn… given its size and consistency") does not hold.

## 7. Hours worked were not measured

Limitation 4 is mentioned and then set aside, but it goes to the heart of the per-hour claim. If staff worked longer days or answered messages on their day off, the true per-hour gain is smaller and could be close to zero. Actual hours were not collected "from all organisations", which implies they were collected from some. Those data should be reported.

## 8. The fatigue explanation is not supported by the paper's own evidence

- **Energy fades.** Self-reported energy rose by 0.61 SD at month 3 but only 0.29 SD at month 6, so more than half the gain faded within the pilot. This pattern fits a novelty or honeymoon effect, and it is not discussed.
- **Process changes are a strong alternative explanation.** Managers described cutting meetings (47 of 58), protecting focus time, simplifying approvals and ending low-value reporting, calling the scheme "a forcing device". These changes could plausibly produce the efficiency gains without any reduction in hours. The data cannot separate the two explanations, yet the Discussion favours fatigue.
- **Survey details are missing.** Response rates and attrition across the three survey waves are not reported. The "productivity higher than before" item has no baseline and asks a leading question.

## 9. Self-selection and attrition run through the whole design

- Organisations volunteered, so they were probably those most confident the scheme would work.
- Nine of 70 (13%) withdrew before the pilot. Those that expected to struggle were most likely to leave, which inflates every result.
- Three managers are missing from the interviews (58 of 61), and the paper does not say whether they came from reverting organisations.
- **Continuation is weak evidence.** These were self-selected organisations, and reverting has its own morale cost.

---

## Summary of the main overclaims

| Claim | Problem |
|---|---|
| "Gains in output per hour in every sector" | Follows from the arithmetic whenever output stays above 80 |
| "Sector-general" | Retail lost 6.9% of output and 50% of retail organisations reverted |
| "100% of the output" | Output fell to 98.7 overall and was below baseline in 5 of 6 sectors |
| Revenue shows no sacrifice | Nominal +1.4% is likely a real decline; 15% of organisations missing |
| Sick days −36% | Largely mechanical (fewer working days) and possibly seasonal |
| Fatigue is the main mechanism | Energy gains faded, and process changes are an equally good explanation |
| Limitations "unlikely to overturn" | The consistency relied on is either arithmetic or shared bias |

## What would strengthen it

1. Lead with the output index, not output per hour, and report its distribution across organisations.
2. Report the continuation and reversion breakdown by sector, and drop or narrow the sector-general claim.
3. Express sick days per scheduled day and match the seasonal comparison periods.
4. Deflate revenue and identify which organisations did not report it.
5. Report actual-hours data wherever it exists.
6. Give survey response rates and present the energy trajectory honestly.
7. Add confidence intervals or any formal uncertainty quantification.

A fair conclusion from these data would be something like this: in self-selected knowledge-work organisations, a 20% cut in scheduled hours was associated with small reported output losses and better wellbeing; in customer-facing sectors the evidence was mixed and reversion was common. That is still an interesting result, but it is not what the Summary currently claims.
